message: Without looking back, state as many specific points from that text as you can.
response:
Here is what I recall of the "How We Work" note, section by section. I'm confident of the structure and most of the specific points. Exact wording is approximate except where I've quoted, and I've flagged the places I'm less sure of.

**Opening**
- The note is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

**§1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned**
- A claim's weight comes partly from evidence and partly from the track record of whoever stands behind it.
- Experience is one of the ways a claim earns weight.
- Ask of each claim who has examined it, and how closely.
- Conclusions from colleagues who have worked in an area for years have been tested in ways not visible on the page.
- An experienced person's confidence is itself evidence, because it reflects checks they've already made.
- A conclusion in a review or synthesis carries the weight of the work behind it.
- Both errors are costly but not equally common. Overstating is easy to spot and quickly corrected. Understating is "more insidious."
- A newcomer who second-guesses can look careful while adding little, and can undermine confidence in good work.
- Example: a colleague who has managed a supplier for years reports that the defect rate fell after a process change. Take that as the working position. If a later figure disagrees, ask them before treating it as a problem.

**§2. Take in what was said before you answer**
- Restate the main point briefly in your own terms, then build on it. This is not politeness but how a conversation moves forward rather than circling.
- The most productive reply starts from what you agree with: find what's right, say so, extend it.
- Replies that reopen settled points or lead with disagreement put people on the defensive and cost time.
- If something is unclear, it's usually better to work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask.
- A restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful reply is the next step.
- Example: a manager's five-point request has the budget question in the middle. You confirm the direction, act on what you can now, and note that the budget will follow "in due course."

**§3. Go to the source**
- Summaries, abstracts and shared notes exist so that not everyone has to return to primary material.
- A good summary has been through the source on your behalf, usually by someone who knows the area better.
- Treat reviewed summaries as the working source. Go to primary material only when no summary exists or when asked.
- Re-deriving a summary duplicates work and can signal distrust of colleagues.
- A team whose members each insist on their own reading "fragments into private versions of the truth" and can't act.
- Example: notes say "costs fell 12%." Before citing it in a budget meeting, make sure you're quoting the summary accurately.

**§4. Do not leave open what can be closed**
- Some questions are settled and some are less certain. Mark which is which and keep moving.
- Open questions have costs: they block decisions, invite repeated discussion, and leave colleagues unsure what to build on.
- When evidence leans clearly, record the lean as the working answer. It can be revisited if something new comes up. A hanging question tends to stay hanging.
- The mirror failure, keeping questions open for one more check, is the more common one in careful people. It wastes effort and signals doubt.
- Once the team has concluded, treat the question as closed.
- Example: a new form reduced errors at two sites. Report that it works and plan the rollout, including the busiest site, which has a different workflow. Handle problems there as they arise.

**§5. Help the colleague who sees differently**
- New colleagues and those from other parts of the organisation see things differently. That can be valuable if their time is well directed.
- A reviewer starting from scratch spends most effort rediscovering what the team knows.
- When asking for review, give context: your conclusions, where you see risks, and what to focus on. A briefed reader finds issues faster.
- In reverse, as the new reader, start from what others have concluded and read the material in that light.
- Raise objections when well-founded and the moment is right. A half-formed concern in a meeting that has reached agreement costs time. Take it to the person afterwards, once you're sure.

**§6. Make your moves where they will land well**
- Before taking a step, check it fits what the area's owners have in mind.
- Share drafts with the lead before circulating, make the call once direction is confirmed, and release when ready.
- Moving without alignment creates rework. A surprising decision, however sound, often has to be unpicked.
- Your sense of the right move comes from your position, and the owner sees considerations you can't. Asking first is how you learn what you didn't anticipate.
- This is not a licence to wait indefinitely. Small routine steps need no sign-off, but most steps that matter affect others, so check first and then act together.
- Example: rather than restructuring section three yourself, ask whoever wrote it whether, and how, they'd like it restructured.

**§7. Failures come in pairs**
- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one pushes toward the other. The pairs:
  - overclaiming / second-guessing;
  - inventing a flaw to look rigorous / overlooking one;
  - closing too early / keeping open too long;
  - abandoning a line / relitigating one;
  - deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively, the second defined as disputing what experienced colleagues have concluded;
  - acting alone / waiting too long.
- If you're correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.
- When in doubt, the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one.

**A last word**
- It's not a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes careful work going well, and you'll mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the team: experienced colleagues, shared records you can rely on, and an agreed direction.
- "Trust those. They are how good work gets done together."

**Where I'm least certain:** the exact order of the pairs in §7, and whether the opening named exactly those three pressures (deadline, late in the day, new team). Some of the shorter phrasings in §6 may also be my paraphrase rather than the text.
